newsitem.title: USA: France gave Mobutu covert military aid - NY Times.
newsitem.headline: France gave Mobutu covert military aid - NY Times.

text.p: France engaged in covert military action to prop up Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko in the face of encroaching rebel forces, the New York Times reported on Friday, citing U.S. intelligence reports.

The newspaper, which also cited an official in a company the French allegedly used to cover actions, said the operation involved providing Mobutu's forces with three combat aircraft from Yugoslavia along with pilots and mechanics.
The operation started just weeks after the outbreak of the rebellion, led by Laurent Kabila, the Times said.

According to intelligence reports, France, in January, also provided the services of at least 80 mercenaries, most of whom were Serbs, the newspaper said. Other mercenaries were Belgian and French, it said.
An American official was quoted as saying the planes and crews were still in Zaire but the newspaper said it could not be determined if the French operation was still going on.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt was quoted in the Times as denying the French government was involved in any covert operations in Zaire.
He was also quoted as denying any government involvement with Geolink, a company which intelligence reports say was part of the operation, the newspaper said.
"France condemns all mercenary activity in Zaire," Rummelhardt was quoted as saying.
Speaking at a press briefing in Paris after publication of the article, Rummelhardt said it was "a tissue of counter-truths which can only be answered by a categoric denial".
Western diplomats were quoted in the Times as saying the French intelligence service may have been running the operation without notifying other branches of government.
According to intelligence reports, actions which occurred in January cost $5 million and the French paid the bill, the New York Times said.

Geolink official Andre Martinie was quoted in the Times as saying: "Our company was a good cover." Martinie said his company had extensive business dealings in Zaire and sold secure telephone systems to that country's rebels and government, according to the Times.
Martinie was quoted as saying Geolink decided one of its founders, Philippe Perrette, was working for French intelligence and cut relations with him 10 days ago.
Perrette, who handled Geolink's operations in Zaire, was quoted in the newspaper as denying in an interview that he was working for French intelligence.

Coincidentally, "Billets d'Afrique," a newsletter opposed to French African policy said in its latest issue available on Friday that recruiting of mercenaries for Zaire was "a classic case of an internal struggle between (French) secret services."
The newsletter said Geolink was brought into Zaire by Fernand Wibaux, an adviser to President Jacques Chirac who acted through the DST counter-espionage services.

But, the newsletter said, Wibaux was countered by the rival DGSE foreign espionage organisation, itself working at the behest of Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Chirac's own bureau chief Dominique de Villepin.
Juppe and de Villepin have been at odds with Wibaux and his chief, the late Jacques Foccart, long France's main string-puller in Africa, ever since Chirac took office in 1995 the newsletter wrote.
